submission.natural_language_explanation: L3/N2714+ is a retrospective detector for the operative verb of an English clause: the token that names a concrete process, operation or transaction applied to a thing - contract, dry, fill, heat, mix, press, cut, measure, weigh, count, pay, hire, buy, sell, ship, load, connect, produce, work, result, last. It needs the word in verb position (the same word used as a noun, or as an -ed/-ing form, gives ~0) and stays near 0 on stative, existential and motion verbs (be, have, seem, remain, continue, persist, endure, grow, expand, walk, come, lose, win, fail); it also fires, more weakly, on the particle that completes such a predicate (up, of, in), and the plain action verbs wash, pull and add are an unexplained leftover that stays low.

Riverside Water Treatment Works has supplied the eastern half of the county since 1968, when the first settling tanks were poured on the floodplain beside the old mill race. The plant draws raw water from the river through two intake screens, and from a pair of boreholes that reach a chalk aquifer about forty metres below the yard. Operators work in three shifts, and the night shift is usually the quietest, because demand from the housing estates drops sharply after midnight and the reservoirs refill themselves.

The treatment train itself is not complicated. Raw water arrives in the reception chamber, passes through coarse and fine screens, and then enters the coagulation stage, where a dilute solution of aluminium sulphate is dosed into the flow. The particles in the river water are mostly clay and organic matter, and they carry a slight negative charge that keeps them apart. The coagulant neutralises that charge, so the particles begin to clump together into larger flocs that will settle out downstream. Nothing in this stage is dramatic; it is a slow chemical nudge rather than a violent reaction.

From the flocculation tanks the water moves to the clarifiers, which are wide, shallow basins with rotating scraper arms at the bottom. Most of the floc settles to the floor within a few hours and is drawn off as sludge, which is thickened and tankered away once a week. The clearer water above the sludge blanket flows over the weirs and on to the filters. Each filter bed is a metre of graded sand over a layer of gravel, and the beds are backwashed every thirty-six hours with a reverse flow of treated water and air.

Disinfection comes last. Chlorine gas is injected into the filtered water at a dose the operators adjust according to the temperature and the organic load, and the water then sits in a covered contact tank for at least half an hour before it can be released. Twice a day a technician will measure the residual chlorine at three points along the contact tank and record each reading in the log. If a reading falls below the target, the dosing rate is raised at once and the shift supervisor is informed.

The laboratory at the far end of the site handles the bacteriological sampling, and its benches are kept deliberately cluttered, because the analysts prefer to keep their glassware within reach rather than in cupboards. Every morning, before the first samples arrive, a lab assistant will mix the growth medium for the coliform plates and pour it into sterile dishes, which then set in a warm room next to the incubator.

Visitors often remark that the whole site smells faintly of bleach and wet stone, and that the noise from the pumps is constant but oddly soothing. The works has never had a serious supply interruption, and the staff would like to keep it that way.
